8.6An Introduction to the Generics Framework

When we compile our Java source code, we often see compilation warnings like this one when we compile our MapExample.java file.

Note: MapExample.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations.

Note: Recompile with -Xlint:unchecked for details.

These warnings occur because we might be using the collections framework without generics. So, what exactly is the generics framework, and how can we use it to eliminate these warnings?

The generics framework was introduced in Java 5, and it provides a way to parameterize types, known as elements. If you look at the Java API documentation for any collection interface or class, you'll notice a diamond operator (<>) with a type parameter, like E (for elements). This is also true for sub-interfaces of collections. For Map, instead of E, we use K and V for key-value pairs.

Generics reduce the amount of code required when adding or retrieving objects from a collection. For instance, in previous examples, when we used an iterator to retrieve objects from a collection, we had to cast the returned object because the next() method returns a generic Object type.

By using generics, we introduce compile-time type safety, allowing the compiler to catch invalid types during compilation. This also eliminates the need for explicit casting. Let's see how this works with a new version of our loop, using generics. Refer to the code below, lines 26 to 31.

You can declare generics in your collection declarations. For example, in a Set declaration, you can specify that it only accepts Person objects using the diamond operator (<>). Both the left-hand and right-hand sides of the declaration should specify the Person type. This ensures that only Person objects can be added to the Set. If you attempt to add a non-Person object, such as a String, it will result in a compilation error. This error helps ensure that only the correct types are added to the collection, and it appears during compile-time, making it easier to debug. Look at the commented line 20 in the code below; using that line will cause an error.

Let’s revisit our test class, TestPerson.java, but this time, it uses the diamond operator (<>).

2

7   Person p1 = new Person("Edwin", 20);

9   Person p3 = new Person("Ericson", 24);

10   Person p4 = new Person("Jerry", 18);

11   Person p5 = new Person("Lesley", 27);

12  

13    Set<Person> myFriends = new HashSet<Person>();

14    

15    myFriends.add(p1);

16    myFriends.add(p2);

17    myFriends.add(p3);

18    myFriends.add(p4);

19    myFriends.add(p5);

21

22  //  System.out.println(myFriends);

23

25  

26    while(it.hasNext()) {

27

31    }

32

33    System.out.println("Sum: " + sum);

37           + averageAge);

Additionally, you can use an enhanced for-loop (also known as a "for-each" loop) to iterate over the collection. The enhanced for-loop is designed specifically for use with collections and arrays. It consists of two parts: the first part is a temporary object (e.g., Person p), and the second part is the collection (myFriends). This loop automatically retrieves each Person object from the collection, making the code even more concise.

Try to use the code snippet below to use the enhanced for loop by changing lines 21 to 31 of the test class TestPerson.java. It should still work, and it should also give you the same output.

  }

8.7The Diamond (<>) Operator

In Java SE7, a new language feature called the diamond operator (<>) was introduced to improve the usability of the Generics framework. Prior to Java SE7, whenever you declared a collection, you had to specify the type of objects that the collection would hold, both on the left-hand side (the declaration) and the right-hand side (the instantiation).

For example, when declaring a Set or List, you needed to specify the type twice, as shown below:

Set<Person> mySet = new HashSet<Person>();

However, with the introduction of the diamond operator in Java SE7, this redundancy is no longer necessary. You can now use the diamond operator on the right-hand side during the instantiation, which allows the compiler to infer the type from the left-hand side. This feature is also applicable to Map objects.

In older versions of Java, you had to repeat the type declaration during both the declaration and instantiation of a Map, like this:

Map<String, Integer> myMap = new HashMap<String, Integer>();

With Java SE7 and later, the diamond operator simplifies this process. Now, you only need to specify the type on the left-hand side during the declaration, and you can use the diamond operator on the right-hand side.

This approach is known as type inference, where the compiler infers the type from the left-hand side declaration. This reduces code redundancy and makes your code more concise.

Let's take a look at an example. Suppose we have the following code that uses the diamond operator:

Set<Person> myFriends = new HashSet<>();

Here, we declare that the Set will hold Person objects, but thanks to the diamond operator, we no longer need to repeat the Person type on the right-hand side. The compiler automatically understands that the HashSet will only contain Person objects.

If we save, compile, and run the code, we will get the same output as before, but with a cleaner and more modern syntax. The diamond operator is a small but powerful addition to Java that enhances the readability and maintainability of your code, especially when working with the Generics framework.

8.8Factory Methods for Immutable Collections (JDK 9)

In JDK 9, the List, Set, and Map interfaces introduced new static factory methods of() and copyOf()to create immutable collections. These methods make it easier and more concise to create fixed collections.

For example:

List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie");

Set<Integer> numbers = Set.of(1, 2, 3);

Map<Integer, String> idToName = Map.of(1, "Apple", 2, "Banana");

The collections created this way are immutable and will throw UnsupportedOperationException if you attempt to modify them. This is especially useful for creating constants or passing data that should not be changed.

8.9Revisiting Local Variable Type Inference using var (JDK 10)

Let us revisit the discussion on JDK 10’s var keyword that was discussed in Chapter 1. The var keyword also allows the compiler to infer the variable type, improving code readability when used with generic collections. This is especially useful when the type is obvious from the right-hand side:

var names = List.of("Jane", "John", "Doe");

var idMap = new HashMap<Integer, String>();

However, developers should use var judiciously to maintain readability, especially in complex declarations.

8.10Collectors.toUnmodifiableList/Set/Map (JDK 10)

In JDK 10, Java introduced new collector methods that make it easier to create read-only collections directly from streams. These are the Collectors.toUnmodifiableList(), Collectors.toUnmodifiableSet(), and Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap() methods.

Before this, you would often collect elements into a regular collection and then wrap it using Collections.unmodifiableList() or similar methods. Now, you can produce an unmodifiable collection in one step, making the code cleaner and less error-prone. An unmodifiable collection cannot be changed after it’s created, any attempt to add, remove, or update an element will result in an UnsupportedOperationException. This is useful when you want to ensure that the result of a stream operation stays consistent and is not altered by mistake elsewhere in your program.

Here’s sample code to demonstrate these new methods:

1   import java.util.List;

2   import java.util.Set;

3   import java.util.Map;

4   import java.util.stream.Collectors;

5   import java.util.stream.Stream;

6  

7   public class UnmodifiableCollectorsExample {

8     public static void main(String[] args) {

9       // Unmodifiable List

10     List<String> names =

11         Stream.of("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")

12        .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());

13     System.out.println("List: " + names);

14

15     // Unmodifiable Set

16     // duplicates are removed

17     Set<Integer> numbers = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 3)

18        .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableSet());

19     System.out.println("Set: " + numbers);

20

21     // Unmodifiable Map

22     Map<Integer, String> idNameMap =

23        Stream.of("A", "B", "C")

24        .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(

25        String::length, // key: length of string

26        value -> value // value: the string itself

27     ));

28     System.out.println("Map: " + idNameMap);

29

30    // Trying to modify will throw an exception

31    // Uncomment to see UnsupportedOperationException

32    // names.add("David");

33   }

34 }

In this example, the stream elements are collected directly into unmodifiable collections without any extra wrapping step. This not only reduces boilerplate code but also helps enforce immutability right at the point of collection, making your data safer from unintended modifications.

8.11Sequenced Collections (JDK 21)

In JDK 21, Java introduced the Sequenced Collection interfaces, which provide a consistent way to work with collections that have a defined encounter order—meaning the elements are stored in a specific sequence. These new interfaces include SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, and SequencedMap. They extend the existing collection types and add methods to easily access the first and last elements, as well as to traverse the collection in reverse order. Before this feature, you had to rely on different collection-specific methods or manual iteration to perform these tasks, which could vary between types. With sequenced collections, you can write code that works the same way for lists, sets, or maps that maintain order, improving readability and consistency.

1   import java.util.SequencedCollection;

2   import java.util.ArrayList;

3  

4   public class SequencedCollectionExample {

5     public static void main(String[] args) {

6      // Creating a sequenced collection

7      // (ArrayList implements SequencedCollection)

8      SequencedCollection<String> fruits

9              = new ArrayList<>();

10    fruits.add("Apple");

11    fruits.add("Banana");

12    fruits.add("Cherry");

13

14    // Accessing first and last elements directly

15    System.out.println("First fruit: "

16                + fruits.getFirst());

17    System.out.println("Last fruit: "

18                + fruits.getLast());

19    // Iterating in reverse order

20    System.out.println("Fruits in reverse:");

21    for (String fruit : fruits.reversed()) {

22       System.out.println(fruit);

23    }

24   }

25 }

Here's the output after execution:

First fruit: Apple
Last fruit: Cherry
Fruits in reverse:
Cherry
Banana
Apple

In this example, we use getFirst() and getLast() to quickly retrieve the first and last elements, and reversed() to loop through the list from end to start—all without writing extra logic. This feature makes working with ordered collections more straightforward and consistent across different collection types.

These enhancements introduced in newer JDK versions build upon the strong foundation of the Java Collections Framework and Generics. They promote immutability, conciseness, and safer type handling, enabling developers to write more expressive and maintainable code.

Chapter Summary

●The Collection interface is the root of the collection hierarchy in Java, representing a group of objects known as its elements and serving as the basis for more specific sub-interfaces like Set and List. While the Java Development Kit (JDK) does not provide direct implementations of this interface, it is widely used for passing and manipulating collections with maximum generality, with details available in the official Java API documentation.

●Collection objects in Java are part of the Collections Framework, offering dynamic data structures like lists, sets, and queues, which can grow or shrink in size and provide various methods for manipulating elements. Arrays, on the other hand, are fixed in size and store elements of a specific data type, offering fewer built-in methods for element manipulation compared to collections.

●The Set interface in Java is designed to store a collection of unordered, unique elements, prohibiting duplicates and allowing at most one null element. When duplicate elements are added to a Set, only the first occurrence is retained, and subsequent duplicates are ignored.

●The List interface represents an ordered collection where the sequence of elements is maintained, allowing duplicates and enabling access by index, unlike the Set interface, which stores unordered, unique elements and disallows duplicates. When comparing examples using List and Set, the List (e.g., ArrayList) preserves the insertion order and includes all elements, while the Set (e.g., HashSet) omits duplicates and does not guarantee order.

●A Map is another data structure that stores elements as key-value pairs, where each key (K) is associated with a corresponding value (V), allowing for efficient retrieval based on the key. Unlike Set and List interfaces, which use a single type parameter (E) for elements, the Map interface uses two type parameters (K and V) to define the types of keys and values it holds.

●The Set, List, and Map interfaces allow adding and printing objects from collections, typically displaying them within square brackets ([]). To format output differently or perform computations while iterating through a collection, you can use the Iterator interface for forward-only iteration, especially with unordered collections like Set, or the ListIterator interface for bidirectional iteration in ordered collections like List.

●The Generics framework significantly improves the usability and safety of the Collections Framework in Java. It eliminates the need for casting when retrieving objects, ensures compile-time type safety, and allows for more concise and readable code. By declaring specific types in your collections, you can create homogeneous sets and avoid runtime errors related to type mismatches.

●The diamond operator (<>) introduced in Java SE7 simplifies the use of the Generics framework by allowing the compiler to infer the type of a collection from its declaration, eliminating the need to repeat the type on both sides of the assignment. This feature reduces redundancy and enhances code readability, as seen in examples like Set<Person> mySet = new HashSet<>();, where the type Person no longer needs to be specified twice.

Coding Task 1: Library Management System Using Java Collections

Task Overview:

Design and implement a basic library management system that can store, manage, and retrieve information about books. You will utilize Java Collections to handle the storage and manipulation of books. Each book in the system should have a unique identifier, a title, an author, and a genre.

Task Breakdown:

1. Creation of the Book Class:

Create a Book class with the following attributes:

●String title

●String author

●String isbn (each book's unique identifier)

●String genre

●Implement constructors, accessor methods, mutator methods, and a toString() method for easy display of book information.

2. Creation of the Library Class:

Use a Set<Book> to maintain the collection of books, ensuring that no two books with the same ISBN can exist in the collection.

Implement the following methods:

●void addBook(Book book): Adds a new book to the library.

●Book searchByISBN(String isbn): Retrieves a book based on its ISBN. Returns null if the book is not found.

●List<Book> searchByAuthor(String author): Returns a list of books by the specified author.

●List<Book> searchByGenre(String genre): Returns a list of books that belong to the specified genre.

●void removeBook(String isbn): Removes a book from the library using its ISBN.

●void displayBooks(): Displays all books in the library using an Iterator.

3. Main Class:

In the main method, showcase the use of the library system by:

●Adding several books to the library.

●Searching for a book by its ISBN.

●Finding books by a particular author or genre.

●Removing a book using its ISBN.

●Displaying all books in the library.

Additional Guidelines:

●Optimize operations for efficiency.

●Handle edge cases, such as attempting to add duplicate books or searching for books that do not exist.

Expected Results:

The program should successfully demonstrate the addition, retrieval, removal, and display of books within the library, using various Java Collections and Generics to manage the operations.

This task challenges students to apply their knowledge of Java Collections (Set, List, Map), Generics, and Iterators in a practical scenario involving the management of a collection of books.

CHAPTER 9

Building Graphical User Interfaces (GUI) in Java

Key Learning Objectives

●Introducing the java.awt package

●Things to consider while building your GUI application

●Learning about Java layout managers

●Understanding layout managers while creating your SimpleCalculator app

This chapter dives into building graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using the components and tools provided in java.awt package. You’ll learn how to incorporate essential GUI elements such as buttons, text fields, labels, and containers to construct user-friendly applications. We'll cover the roles of panels, frames, and dialogs, as well as introduce Java’s various layout managers, such as FlowLayout, BorderLayout, and GridLayout, which help arrange components in a visually appealing manner. As we explore customizing layout managers, you will apply these concepts by building and refining a simple calculator application.

9.1Introducing the java.awt Package

Welcome to the Java AWT (Abstract Window Toolkit) section, an essential part of the Java API. The AWT package allows you to create graphical user interface (GUI) components like buttons, frames, text fields, text areas, and more. It's important to note that AWT was the original GUI toolkit included when Java 1.0 was first released, marking it as a first-generation toolkit.

As Java evolved, the second-generation user interface toolkit called Swing was introduced, providing more advanced features and flexibility. In addition to AWT and Swing, Java now also offers JavaFX, another powerful toolkit for creating rich user interfaces. However, for this discussion, we'll focus on AWT.

To begin with, let's revisit a fundamental concept: in Java, the Object class is the root of all class hierarchies. One of the subclasses of Object is the Component class, which represents anything visual that you can interact with in a user interface. Examples of components include buttons, labels, checkboxes, choice boxes, list boxes, and even containers.

Figure 9.1 The AWT Class Hierarchy

Figure 9.1 illustrates the class hierarchy of Java’s Abstract Window Toolkit (AWT). At the top of the hierarchy is the Object class, from which all AWT components inherit. The Component class serves as the root for all graphical UI elements such as Button, Label, Checkbox, Choice, and List. These are individual user interface components.

The Container class, which also inherits from Component, can hold other components and containers, making it essential for creating complex UI layouts. Container branches into two main types:

●Window-based containers, such as Frame and Dialog, which are independent containers that do not need to be embedded in another UI component.

●Panel-based containers, such as Panel and Applet, which are dependent containers and must be added to a window or another container to be displayed.

This hierarchy shows how AWT organizes reusable and extendable UI components for building graphical user interfaces in Java applications.

Among these, the Container class is particularly important because it allows you to hold and organize other components within it. For example, you can place a button inside a container. Two common subclasses of the Container class are Window and Panel.

A Window is a type of container that can exist independently. Once you create a window, it can run on its own without needing any other containers. On the other hand, a Panel is also a container but cannot exist independently. It must be placed inside another container, such as a window or an applet, to function properly.

For instance, you can create a Frame (which is a type of window) and launch it by itself. However, if you create a Panel, it won't run on its own. Instead, it needs to be added to a frame or another container.

Each container in AWT comes with a default layout manager that controls how the components within it are arranged.

It's also worth noting that the Applet class, which was introduced in Java 1.1, is only supported up to Java 8. From Java 9 onwards, the Applet class has been deprecated, and as of Java 17, they have been completely removed.

Now, let's take a closer look at the AWT package. It includes several interfaces and classes that you'll frequently use in building GUIs. For example, the Button class allows you to create clickable buttons, while the Checkbox class lets you create selectable checkboxes. The Frame class, as mentioned earlier, is used to create window components that can stand alone. By understanding and utilizing these components and containers effectively, you'll be able to create functional and user-friendly graphical interfaces in Java.

9.2Things to Consider While Building Your GUI Application

After exploring the java.awt package, which includes the essential classes for building graphical user interface (GUI) applications in Java, let us explore the three main categories: components, containers, and layout managers.

1.Components are the visual elements of your application, such as buttons, frames, dialog boxes, text areas, and text fields. These are the parts of your application that users will interact with directly.

2.Containers are a special type of component. Like other components, they are visual elements, but their main purpose is to hold and organize other components within them. Examples of containers include frames and panels.

3.Layout managers determine how the components are arranged within a container. They control the positioning and sizing of components inside containers, ensuring that your application’s interface is organized and easy to use.

9.2.1The Frame Class

Let’s dive into the Frame class, which is a fundamental part of creating graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in Java. A frame is a top-level window that includes a border and a title bar, making it a container that can hold other GUI components.

By default, frames use a layout manager called BorderLayout. However, you can easily change this layout manager to suit your needs, and we’ll explore how to do that shortly. Frames are resizable, meaning you can adjust their size using the corners of the window.

Now, let’s look at a sample code that demonstrates how to create a simple GUI using a frame. To begin, look at the source code provided at the end of this discussion, saved as SampleFrame.java. In the provided source code, we must import the necessary package, which is java.awt located on line 1.

In the sample code, a Frame object is declared, and the constructor and methods are defined in lines 9 to 12. This approach is the best practice when building a GUI application. First, you declare all your components and containers. Then, within the constructor, you initialize them, just like in the provided code. Finally, you define methods to manage the behavior of these components.

In the startApp() method, which is a user-defined method, we set up the properties for the frame. For example, we set the background color to yellow using setBackground(Color.YELLOW), and we specify the size of the frame as 200 pixels wide and 200 pixels high using setSize(200, 200). You may check the API documentation to see the common Color objects, which you can see under the java.awt.Color class.

Table 9.1 shows the predefined colors available in Java's java.awt.Color class, along with its corresponding RGB values. These colors can be accessed using constants from the Color class, such as Color.RED, Color.BLUE or through the constructor call, ie, new Color (0, 255, 0) for Green.

Table 9.1 Common Color Names and Their RGB Values

Color Red Green Blue RGB Value
Black 0 0 0 (0, 0, 0)

Gray 128 128 128 (128, 128, 128)

By default, frames are invisible when first created. It’s crucial to call the setVisible(true) method, which makes the frame visible. Without this, your GUI will run, but you won’t see anything on the screen.

After running the code, you’ll see how the frame looks on your screen. Remember, the appearance of your GUI might slightly differ depending on whether you are using Windows, macOS, or another operating system.

Here's a simple example code for creating a basic frame. The source code below is saved as SampleFrame.java.

Here’s the runtime output of SampleFrame.java:

Figure 9.2 Runtime Output of SampleFrame.java

Frames in Java are containers, but there are also other containers, such as panels. Panels provide a space where you can place other components, but unlike frames, they cannot be launched on their own. Panels must be added to another container, like a frame.

In our next example, we will create both a frame and a panel. We set the frame's size to 400 by 200 pixels and its background color to yellow. We also create a panel with a size of 100 by 100 pixels and a purple background. Panels are placed inside frames using the add() method.

The setBackground() method changes the background color of a container, using either predefined colors like Color.YELLOW or custom colors by specifying RGB values. The RGB values range from 0 to 255 for each of the red, green, and blue components.

If you want to disable the default layout manager (which is BorderLayout for frames), you can call setLayout(null) to disable the layout manager. Then, you can manually position your components inside the frame.

Here's a simple example code for creating a basic frame and a panel. The source code below is saved as PanelInsideAFrame.java.

1 import java.awt.*;

2

3  public class PanelInsideAFrame {

4    private Frame f;

5    private Panel p;

6

7    public PanelInsideAFrame() {

8        f = new Frame("Panel in a Frame");

9        p = new Panel();

10    }

11

12    public void startApp() {

9.3Java Layout Managers

Let's discuss layout managers, which are tools used in Java to arrange and position components within containers. These managers help control how your components are displayed on the screen.

For more complex layouts, you can nest containers, which means placing one container inside another, allowing you to create customized layouts. In the java.awt package, there are five main layout managers: FlowLayout, BorderLayout, GridLayout, CardLayout, and GridBagLayout. Additionally, the Swing package offers two more layout managers: BoxLayout and SpringLayout.

9.3.1The FlowLayout Manager

Let's start by understanding how the FlowLayout manager works. FlowLayout arranges components in a row, much like words in a line of text. By default, it arranges buttons or similar components in a horizontal line until it runs out of space, at which point it moves to the next line. The alignment of these lines can be adjusted using properties like LEFT, RIGHT, CENTER, LEADING, and TRAILING.

Here’s an example to illustrate this. Imagine you have four buttons. With FlowLayout, if only two buttons fit in the first row, the third button automatically moves to the next row, and so on. If you resize the window (the container), the buttons will adjust themselves to fit the new size.

Below is a sample code demonstrating the use of FlowLayout: The filename is FlowLayoutExample.java.

1    import java.awt.*;

2  

3    public class FlowLayoutExample {

4  

5      // Attributes

6       private Frame f;

7       private Button addBtn, subBtn, mulBtn, divBtn;

8  

9       // Constructor

10     public FlowLayoutExample() {

11        f = new Frame("Flow Layout Example");

12        addBtn = new Button("+");

13        subBtn = new Button("-");

14        mulBtn = new Button("*");

15        divBtn = new Button("/");

16     }

17

18     // Methods

19     public void startApp() {

20       // setting FlowLayout as the layout manager

21       f.setLayout(new FlowLayout());    

22       f.add(addBtn);

23       f.add(subBtn);

24       f.add(mulBtn);

25       f.add(divBtn);

26       f.setSize(200, 200);

27       f.setVisible(true);

28     }

29

30     public static void main(String[] args) {

31       FlowLayoutExample example

32             = new FlowLayoutExample();

33       example.startApp();

34     }

35  }

When we try to compile and run the code, we’ll have this output below. Try resizing the frame horizontally and vertically, and observe how the buttons are realigned within the frame. The images below show the different versions of the Frame when resized.

Figure 9.4 FlowLayout Sample Output 1

Figure 9.5 FlowLayout Sample Output 2

Figure 9.6 FlowLayout Sample Output 3

In this code, we create a frame and four buttons. Each button is labeled with a mathematical operator: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. After declaring and initializing the frame and buttons, we set the layout of the frame to FlowLayout using f.setLayout(new FlowLayout());. This line is crucial because if omitted, the frame will default to BorderLayout, which arranges components differently.

Once the layout manager is set, we add the buttons to the frame using the add() method. Finally, we set the size of the frame to 200x200 pixels and make it visible with f.setVisible(true);.

After compiling and running this code, you will see a window with four buttons arranged according to the FlowLayout. If you resize the window, you will notice how the buttons automatically reposition themselves to fit the available space.

FlowLayout also allows you to specify the alignment of the components within the layout. By default, the alignment is centered, but you can change it by passing a different alignment constant, like FlowLayout.LEFT or FlowLayout.RIGHT when setting the layout.

This is just one example of a layout manager provided by the java.awt package, and it gives you a glimpse of how powerful and flexible layout managers can be in organizing your GUI components.

9.3.2The BorderLayout Manager

The next layout manager that we’re going to explore is the default layout manager used in Java frames, known as the BorderLayout. This layout manager divides a container into five regions: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST, and CENTER. When arranging components in a BorderLayout, each region can hold only one component, and each region is specified by its corresponding constant (e.g., BorderLayout.NORTH, BorderLayout.SOUTH, etc.).

If you don’t specify a region when adding a component, it will automatically be placed in the CENTER region. This region is the default and is the only one that can expand both horizontally and vertically. Components in the NORTH and SOUTH regions only resize horizontally, while those in the EAST and WEST regions only resize vertically.

Figure 9.7 BorderLayout Manager

Let’s go through an example. Suppose we have a frame with five buttons: button-north (bNorth), button-south (bSouth), button-center (bCenter), button-west (bWest), and button-east (bEast). In the constructor of our class, we would first create the frame and the buttons.

Here’s a sample code with a filename: BorderLayoutExample.java.

1    import java.awt.*;

2  

3    public class BorderLayoutExample

4    {

5      private Frame f;

6      private Button bNorth, bSouth, bCenter, bWest, bEast;

7    

8      public BorderLayoutExample()

9      {

10        f = new Frame("BorderLayout Example");

11

12        bNorth = new Button("North");

13        bSouth = new Button("South");  

14        bCenter = new Button("Center");

15        bWest = new Button("West");

16        bEast = new Button("East");

17    }

18  

19    public void startApp()

20    {

21     // frames are using BorderLayout by default,

22     // there's no need to change the layout manager

23     // of the Frame f;

24    

25     f.add(bNorth, BorderLayout.NORTH);

26     f.add(bSouth, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

27     f.add(bCenter, BorderLayout.CENTER);

28     f.add(bWest, BorderLayout.WEST);

29     f.add(bEast, BorderLayout.EAST);

30  

31     f.setSize(400, 200);

32     f.setVisible(true);

33    }

34

35    public static void main(String args[])

36    {

37      BorderLayoutExample be

38             = new BorderLayoutExample();

39      be.startApp();

40    }

41  }

Next, we use a method, let’s call it startApp(), to set up our frame. Since BorderLayout is the default layout manager for frames, we don’t need to call the setLayout() method as we did in the previous example. Instead, we can directly add the buttons to the frame, making sure to specify their positions.

If you forget to specify the region when adding a button, all buttons will stack on top of each other in the CENTER region, and only the last one added will be visible. To avoid this, always specify the correct region for each button.

When you run this code, you will see a frame with five buttons, each located in one of the five regions. If you resize the window horizontally, only the buttons in the NORTH, CENTER, and SOUTH regions will resize. If you resize the window vertically, only the buttons in the WEST, CENTER, and EAST regions will resize. The buttons in the NORTH and SOUTH regions will not change size when the window is resized vertically.

Figure 9.8 BorderLayoutExample.java Runtime Output

9.3.3The GridLayout Manager

The GridLayout manager arranges components within a container in the form of a rectangular grid. The container is divided into equal-sized cells, with one component placed in each cell. When the container is resized, all the components within it remain equally sized, adjusting to fit the new size.

For example, let’s say you have six buttons and you place them inside a frame that uses GridLayout. No matter how you resize the frame, all six buttons will adjust their size equally to fit within the frame. This makes GridLayout a great choice for building applications like a Minesweeper game or a calculator, where you need a consistent grid of buttons.

Now, let's look at a sample code saved as GridLayoutExample.java. In this example, we have a frame and six buttons. Inside the constructor, we create the frame and the six buttons.

1   import java.awt.*;

2  

3   public class GridLayoutExample

4   {

5      private Frame f;

6      private Button b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6;

7    

8      public GridLayoutExample()

9      {

10                 f = new Frame("GridLayout Example");

11

12                 b1 = new Button("B1");

13                 b2 = new Button("B2");

14                 b3 = new Button("B3");

15                 b4 = new Button("B4");

16                 b5 = new Button("B5");

17                 b6 = new Button("B6");

18     }

19  

20    public void startApp()

21    {

22        // to set the layout manager of our Frame f;

23        f.setLayout(new GridLayout(3, 2));

24  

25        // put all the buttons inside the frame,

26        // left --> right

27        // top --> bottom

28  

29        f.add(b1);

30        f.add(b2);

31        f.add(b3);

32        f.add(b4);

33        f.add(b5);

34        f.add(b6);

35  

36        f.pack();

37        f.setVisible(true);

38    }

39

40    public static void main(String args[])

41    {

42        GridLayoutExample ge = new GridLayoutExample();

43        ge.startApp();

44    }

45  }

By default, frames use BorderLayout, so we need to change this by calling the setLayout() method on our frame and setting it to new GridLayout(). When creating a GridLayout, you can pass either two or four integer values to its constructor. In line 23 in the code, we used new GridLayout(3, 2), which means that the layout manager will set up 3 rows and 2 columns.

If you don’t pass any values in the constructor, the layout manager will create a single row with one component per column by default. However, in our code example, we passed two integer values to the constructor. These values specify the number of rows and columns for the grid. Alternatively, you can also specify the horizontal gap (hGap) and vertical gap (vGap) between components, which are measured in pixels.

In our example, we’ve set up the grid with 3 rows and 2 columns. When we add the buttons to the frame, they are arranged from left to right, top to bottom.

Instead of setting the size of the frame manually with f.setSize(), you can use a method called f.pack(). The pack() method automatically sizes the frame just large enough to fit all the components. If you have more components, the frame becomes larger; if you have fewer components, the frame will be smaller.

Finally, we set the frame to be visible by calling setVisible(true). Now let’s save and compile this code and run it.

Figure 9.9 GridLayoutExample.java Runtime Output 1

You can also resize the Frame with GridLayout as its layout manager. As you can see, each region is resized uniformly.

Figure 9.10 GridLayoutExample.java Runtime Output 2

Figure 9.11 GridLayoutExample.java Runtime Output 3

Here’s what happens: The frame displays six equally sized buttons. If you resize the frame, you’ll notice that all the buttons resize equally to fit the new dimensions.

But what happens if you have fewer buttons than the grid allows? For example, what if you only had five buttons instead of six? The frame will still display a 3x2 grid, but the last cell will be left empty.

The same happens if you only have four buttons. The grid layout will still maintain the 3x2 structure, with the extra spaces left blank.

If you try to add more than 6 buttons, the GridLayout will automatically add an extra column to accommodate the additional components. Therefore, the 7th button (and any additional ones) will be placed in a new column, altering the original layout of 3 rows and 2 columns.

When considering: FlowLayout, BorderLayout, and GridLayout, always remember that FlowLayout is the default layout manager for a Panel, while BorderLayout is the default for a Frame.

Chapter Summary

●Java's Abstract Window Toolkit (AWT) is the original API for creating graphical user interfaces, providing components like buttons, frames, and text fields. While newer toolkits like Swing and JavaFX offer more advanced features, this discussion focuses on AWT, where all visual elements are derived from the Component class, a subclass of Object.

●When building a Java GUI application, you’ll work with components (like buttons and text fields), containers (which organize these components, such as frames and panels), and layout managers (which control their arrangement). Understanding how these elements interact is crucial for designing effective user interfaces.

●Java layout managers control the arrangement and size of components within a container, ensuring a consistent layout regardless of screen size or resolution. They provide various ways to organize GUI elements, such as arranging them in a grid, flowing them in a row, or positioning them in specific regions of a container. You can use any of the AWT layout managers (FlowLayout, BorderLayout, GridLayout, CardLayout, or GridBagLayout).

●Customizing layout managers in Java allows you to create tailored layouts by combining different managers or creating your own. This flexibility lets you design unique and complex interfaces that suit specific application needs beyond the standard layout options. This is usually achieved by nesting different layout managers together.

Event Handling Techniques

Key Learning Objectives

●Learn how to implement listener interfaces to respond to various user actions

This chapter dives into the core principles of event-handling techniques in Java, providing a solid foundation for managing user interactions in graphical applications. You'll begin by exploring the Delegation Event Model, where an event source delegates the handling of events to a listener—allowing for cleaner, modular code.

We will cover the fundamentals of event handlers and examine different ways to respond to events using listener interfaces, as well as simplified strategies through adapter classes, inner classes, and anonymous classes. These techniques help you control program behavior based on user actions such as button clicks, mouse movements, or key presses.

To modernize your approach, we will also introduce lambda expressions, which allow for more concise and readable event-handling logic. By the end of the chapter, you will apply what you’ve learned by building a simple calculator, giving you practical experience in designing interactive, event-driven Java applications.

10.1Fundamentals Of Event Handlers

Let’s dive into the basics of event handling in Java. Events are simply objects that describe actions or occurrences, such as clicking a button, moving a mouse, or pressing keyboard shortcuts like CTRL-S. These user interactions are called events because they initiate something within the interface. Each interaction is tied to an event source, which refers to the component involved in the interaction, such as a button, window, or icon.

Figure 10.1 Event Handling Process Diagram

Figure 10.1 illustrates Java’s Event Delegation Model, which is the foundation for handling events in graphical user interfaces. In this model, an Event Source is a component, such as a button, that generates events. An Event Listener is an object that wants to respond to those events. To do so, the listener must implement a specific Listener Interface, which defines the required event-handling methods. The listener is then registered to the event source, establishing a connection where the event source notifies the listener when an event occurs. This setup supports a one-to-many relationship, allowing a single event source to notify multiple listeners. By separating the event generation from its handling, the delegation model promotes a cleaner, more modular design.

For example, in a Word document, clicking the bold button or using the shortcut CTRL-B both trigger events. The components responsible for generating these events are known as event sources, and they notify listeners whenever an event occurs. Each event is encapsulated in an event object, and Java’s java.util.EventObject class is the parent for all event objects, with subclasses like ActionEvent and WindowEvent.

Various components in your interface can produce different types of events. Buttons typically generate ActionEvent objects, while Windows may send WindowEvent objects. To understand these interactions better, you can explore the java.awt package, where you’ll find the necessary classes and interfaces to work with events. Different types of events, like ActionEvent, AdjustmentEvent, and FocusEvent, exist for various kinds of user interactions.

When an ActionEvent occurs, such as clicking a button or pressing the spacebar, the event is triggered, and an event handler responds. Event handlers are methods designed to manage the event and execute the intended behavior. So, for instance, clicking the bold button or pressing CTRL-B both trigger the same event handler to make text bold. These event handlers ensure that, regardless of how you interact with a component, the desired action is performed.

10.2Event Handling Techniques

When a user interacts with a specific user interface component, known as the event source, an appropriate method, referred to as an event handler, handles the interaction. In the following sections, we will explore different techniques to create event handlers.

10.2.1The Event Delegation Model

These techniques include the delegation model, which involves using listeners or interfaces, adapter or abstract classes, and defining inner classes within other classes to handle events. This approach allows you to delegate the event-handling logic to separate classes, resulting in a loosely coupled structure between the GUI components and the event handler logic. Each event handler class can reside in its own Java source file, promoting modularity and maintainability. You can create as many event handlers as needed; however, after defining them, it is essential to register them properly so they can respond to the events generated by the GUI components.

Figure 10.2 illustrates the Event Delegation Model in Java. When a user interacts with a component—such as clicking a button in a graphical user interface (GUI)—an event is generated, specifically an ActionEvent in this case. Instead of the button handling the event itself, the event is delegated to one or more external event handlers that implement the actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) method. These handlers contain the logic to respond to the user's action. This model promotes a clean separation between the GUI and the event-handling logic, allowing different classes or methods to process the same event in various ways depending on how they are registered.

Figure 10.2 The Event Delegation Model

This is the source code for your GUI, saved as: MyGUI.java

1    // MyGUI.java

2  import java.awt.*;

3  public class MyGUI

4  {

5    private Frame f;

6    private Button b;

7

9    public MyGUI()

10    {

11        f = new Frame("Delegation Event Model");

12        b = new Button("Click me!");

13    }

14

15    public void startApp()

16    {

17        f.add(b);

18        f.pack();

19        f.setVisible(true);

20

21        // register your event handler

22

23        // this is event registration #1

24        b.addActionListener(new MyEvent());

25

26        // this is event registration #2

27        b.addActionListener(new MyEventToo());

28    }

29

30    public static void main(String args[])

31    {

32        MyGUI m = new MyGUI();

33        m.startApp();

34    }

35  }

Here’s the source code for your event handler, saved as: MyEvent.java. This file was registered in MyGUI.java in line 24.

1    // MyEvent.java

2    import java.awt.event.*;

3

4    public class MyEvent implements ActionListener {

5        public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {

6        System.out.println("I was clicked!");

7        }

8    }

Here’s another source code for our second event handler, saved as: MyEventToo.java. This file was registered in MyGUI.java in line 27.

1    // MyEventToo.java

2    import java.awt.event.*;

3    public class MyEventToo implements ActionListener {

4        public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {

5          System.out.println("I was piggy backing!");

6        }

7    }

You can create as many event handlers as you want, and they will all work as long as you register them with your GUI component.

10.2.2The Use of Listeners

Listeners are interfaces. If you can recall the rules on interfaces, once you implement an interface, you are required to override ALL the methods in the interface. Table 10.1 shows the commonly used interfaces in the java.awt.event package.

10.2.3The Use of Adapter Classes

There are situations when it is better to use adapter classes rather than listeners. Not all listeners have a corresponding adapter class. Only listeners that contain two or more methods have a corresponding adapter class. For example, if you implement WindowListener, you are required to override all seven methods even if you only need one. If this is the case, it is better to use the WindowAdapter instead.

Here’s a sample code on how to use an adapter class with a file named SampleAdapter.java:

1    import java.awt.*;

2    import java.awt.event.*;

3  

4    public class SampleAdapter extends WindowAdapter

5    {

6      private Frame f;

7      private TextField tf;

8      private Label label;

9  

10    public SampleAdapter()

11    {

12       f = new Frame("A sample adapter code");

13       tf = new TextField(30);

14       label = new Label("You can quit this app");

15    }

16

17     public void startApp()

18    {

19       f.add(label, BorderLayout.NORTH);

20       f.add(tf, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

21

22        f.setSize(300, 200);

23        f.setVisible(true);

24

25        f.addWindowListener(this);

26     }

27

28    public void windowClosing(WindowEvent we)

29    {

30        System.exit(0);

31    }

32

33    public static void main(String args[])

34    {

35       SampleAdapter sa = new SampleAdapter();

36        sa.startApp();

37     }

38  }

10.2.4Inner Classes

The purpose of inner classes is to make tightly coupled components. As for GUI apps, it is used to group the UI code and event handler code together in a single code base.

In an AWT GUI application, an inner class is often used for event handling because it allows the event listener to access the outer class’s methods and fields without requiring additional references. This makes the code more organized and easier to manage. By defining an event handler as an inner class, the event-handling logic remains encapsulated within the main class, reducing clutter and improving readability. Additionally, since an inner class can access private members of its enclosing class, it simplifies interactions with UI components. For example, if a button click needs to update a label or change another component’s state, an inner class can do this directly without requiring extra methods or references. This approach keeps the event-handling code close to the components it manages, making the application more structured and maintainable.

Using inner classes for event handling in AWT apps can make the code cleaner and more organized. An inner class can directly access the variables and methods of the outer class, which means you don't need to pass additional parameters to work with components. This reduces the amount of boilerplate code and makes the event-handling logic easier to understand and maintain. Additionally, because the inner class is tied to the outer class, it can be used specifically for handling events of that particular instance, keeping related code together.

Here’s how we can implement inner classes in building your GUI app.

10.2.5Anonymous Classes

Anonymous classes allow you to create objects on the fly without giving them a formal name. These objects act as event handlers that do not require a separate class reference. Once the event handler has been executed, the anonymous object is automatically discarded, helping to conserve memory and improve performance.

This approach is particularly useful in building efficient mobile or desktop applications, where minimizing memory usage is key to ensuring smoother runtime performance. By reducing the number of active objects, the system can run more efficiently.

The general syntax for using an anonymous class is as follows:

// Syntax for anonymous class

ClassOrInterface obj = new ClassOrInterface() {

    // Override methods or add new code here

};

Here’s a sample of how to implement anonymous classes in your GUI app.

1    // SampleAnonymousClassImplementation.java

2    import java.awt.*;

3    import java.awt.event.*;

4    

5    public class SampleAnonymousClassImplementation {

6       private Frame f;

8       private Label label;

9  

10     public SampleAnonymousClassImplementation() {

11        f = new Frame("A sample anonymous code");

12        tf = new TextField(30);

13        label = new Label("You can quit this app");

14     }

15  

16     public void startApp() {

17        f.add(label, BorderLayout.NORTH);

18        f.add(tf, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

19

20        f.setSize(300, 200);

21        f.setVisible(true);

22

23        // Using an anonymous class for event handling

24        f.addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {

25          public void windowClosing(WindowEvent we) {

26             System.exit(0);

27          }

28        });

29     }

30  

31     public static void main(String args[]) {

32        SampleAnonymousClassImplementation saci =

33           new SampleAnonymousClassImplementation();

34        saci.startApp();

35     }

36  }

SampleAnonymousClassImplementation.java, we used an anonymous class declaration in lines 23 to 28.

10.2.6The Use of Lambda Expression

Lambda expressions allow you to pass functions without names as arguments to methods. This provides a cleaner, more concise way to handle events compared to anonymous classes, making event handling simpler and more readable.

The general syntax for the use of the lambda expression is as follows:

component.addEventListener(event -> {

    // Code to handle the event

});

Here are two examples, with a single statement:

b.addActionListener(

     e -> System.out.println("Handled by "

              + "Lambda Expression"));

Here’s with multiple statements:

b.addActionListener(

   e -> {

     System.out.println("My Event Handler");

     System.out.println("Handled by "

        + "Lambda Expression");

   }

);

10.3Building a SimpleCalculator App With Event Handlers

After we’ve built the structure of the SimpleCalculator app in the previous chapter using components from the java.awt package. The calculator consists of labels, text fields for input, and buttons for arithmetic operations. However, at this stage, the calculator is only a static interface—it doesn’t perform any calculations yet. We are now ready to complete it by including the event handlers.

Our calculator’s functionality is housed inside a constructor, where all the components are created. A method called startApp() arranges these components within the frame using a layout manager. Currently, the calculator looks functional, but doesn’t respond to any user interactions. Clicking on any button (such as +, -, *, /) won’t produce results, and the close button won't work either. Why? Because we haven’t implemented any event handling yet.

Implementing Event Handling

To make the buttons functional, we need to implement event handling. Specifically, we’ll use an ActionListener to capture button clicks. The ActionListener interface is part of the java.awt.event package, and it requires us to override the actionPerformed() method, which handles the action events.

Let’s add this to our code before the main() method. The actionPerformed() method will determine which button was clicked by calling the getSource() method. Once we know the source of the event (the button), we can perform the appropriate action, whether it's adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing the numbers entered in the text fields.

Here’s the actual code:

1  // SimpleCalculator.java

2  import java.awt.*;

3  import java.awt.event.*;

4

5  public class SimpleCalculator implements ActionListener {

6    // Containers

7    private Frame f;

8    private Panel p1, p2, p3, p4;

9

10   // Components

11     private Label l1, l2, l3;

12     private TextField tf1, tf2, tf3;

13     private Button bAdd, bSub, bMul, bDiv, bClear;

14  

15     public SimpleCalculator() {

16       // Frame and Panels

17       f = new Frame("Simple Calculator");

18

19       p1 = new Panel();

20       p2 = new Panel();

21       p3 = new Panel();

22       p4 = new Panel();

23  

24       // Labels and Text Fields

25       l1 = new Label("First Number: ");

26       l2 = new Label("Second Number: ");

27       l3 = new Label("Result: ");

28  

29       tf1 = new TextField("0.0", 15);

30       tf2 = new TextField("0.0", 15);

31       tf3 = new TextField("0.0", 15);

32

33       // Buttons

34       bAdd = new Button("+");

35       bSub = new Button("-");

36       bMul = new Button("*");

37       bDiv = new Button("/");

38       bClear = new Button("C");

39     }

40

41     public void startApp() {

42       // Layout setup

43       p1.add(l1);

44       p1.add(tf1);

45       p2.add(l2);

46       p2.add(tf2);

47       p3.add(l3);

48       p3.add(tf3);

49       p4.add(bAdd);

50       p4.add(bSub);

51       p4.add(bMul);

52       p4.add(bDiv);

53       p4.add(bClear);

54

55       f.setLayout(new GridLayout(4, 1));

56       f.add(p1);

57       f.add(p2);

58       f.add(p3);

59       f.add(p4);

60       f.pack();

61       f.setVisible(true);

62

63       // Register event listeners for buttons

64       bAdd.addActionListener(this);

65       bSub.addActionListener(this);

66       bMul.addActionListener(this);

67       bDiv.addActionListener(this);

68       bClear.addActionListener(this);

69     f.addWindowListener(new MyCloseButtonHandler());

70     }

71  

72     // Event handler for button clicks

73     public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {

74        Object source = e.getSource();

75        double num1 = 0.0, num2 = 0.0, num3 = 0.0;

76  

77        if (!tf1.getText().isEmpty() &&

78          tf2.getText().isEmpty()) {

79          num1 = Double.parseDouble(tf1.getText());

80          num2 = Double.parseDouble(tf2.getText());

81

82          if (source == bAdd) {

83             num3 = num1 + num2;

84          } else if (source == bSub) {

85             num3 = num1 - num2;

86          } else if (source == bMul) {

87             num3 = num1 * num2;

88          } else if (source == bDiv) {

89             num3 = num1 / num2;

90          } else if (source == bClear) {

91             tf1.setText("0.0");

92             tf2.setText("0.0");

93             tf3.setText("0.0");

94          }

95          tf3.setText(String.valueOf(num3));

96        }

97     }

98

99     // Window close handler

100     private class MyCloseButtonHandler

101             extends WindowAdapter {

102      public void windowClosing(WindowEvent we) {

103          System.exit(0);

104       }

105    }

106    public static void main(String[] args) {

107       SimpleCalculator sc = new SimpleCalculator();

108       sc.startApp();

109    }

110  }

Chapter Summary

●Event handling in Java involves interactions such as button clicks, mouse movements, or keyboard shortcuts, which are captured as events and tied to specific components called event sources. Each event triggers a method, known as an event handler, that executes the desired action, ensuring consistent behavior across different types of user interactions.

●There are different event handling techniques, namely the delegation model, using the listener interface, using adapter classes, inner classes, anonymous classes, and using the lambda expression.

CHAPTER 11

Building a Swing Desktop App

Key Learning Objectives

●Understand the key differences between AWT and Swing in Java GUI development

●Learn how to convert AWT applications into Swing-based applications

●Explore commonly used Swing components, such as JCheckBox, JRadioButton, JComboBox, JList, and JLabel

●Gain hands-on experience in designing graphical user interfaces using Swing

●Learn how to package and distribute your Swing applications as Java Archive (JAR) files

In our final chapter, we explore the key differences between AWT and Swing, focusing on how Swing offers a more flexible and modern approach to building graphical user interfaces in Java. While AWT laid the foundation for GUI development, Swing enhances it with a richer set of components and greater control over look and feel. You'll learn how to transition an existing AWT-based application into a Swing-based one, unlocking more advanced features and improved visual design. We’ll also take a closer look at several commonly used Swing components—such as JCheckBox, JRadioButton, JComboBox, JList, and JLabel—and see how they can enhance user interaction. Finally, the chapter will guide you through packaging your Swing application into a Java Archive (JAR) file, making it easy to share, run, or deploy across platforms. By the end of this chapter, you’ll be ready to design, build, and distribute full-featured Java desktop applications using Swing.

11.1AWT vs. Swing

Java AWT (Abstract Window Toolkit) and Swing are both used for building graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in Java, but they have key differences.

Swing is part of the Java Foundation Classes (JFC) and is built on top of AWT. While AWT relies on native operating system components, Swing provides lightweight, platform-independent components that look the same across all operating systems.

In AWT, components like Frame and Button are directly tied to the platform, meaning their appearance can vary depending on whether you're using Windows, macOS, or Linux. In contrast, Swing components like JFrame and JButton look consistent across different platforms since they don't depend on the native OS.

Figure 11.1 AWT Sample Frame for both Solaris and Windows OS

Figure 11.2 Swing Sample Frame

Swing adds more features and flexibility. It offers additional components like JRadioButton, JComboBox, JCheckBox, and JLabel, which are not available in AWT. Swing also supports a pluggable look-and-feel, meaning you can customize the appearance of components, something AWT does not support.

Another key difference is that AWT components are generally heavier in memory and slower, while Swing components are lightweight, offering better performance. Swing also follows the MVC (Model-View-Controller) design pattern, which AWT doesn't support.

In summary, AWT provides basic, platform-dependent components, while Swing offers a richer, more flexible, and platform-independent set of components. Swing was also introduced in Java 1.2 to replace the AWT package.

11.2Converting Your AWT App to a Swing-Based App

In this section, we will focus on converting an AWT (Abstract Window Toolkit) application into a basic Swing-based application. To achieve this, it is essential to import the javax.swing package into our simple calculator application.

As a brief recap, the original calculator application utilizes various AWT components, including panels, frames, labels, text fields, and buttons. It also incorporates the AWT event package to manage event handling, such as using an ActionListener to respond to button clicks or implementing a close button handler that enables the application to close when the user presses Command+Q (for macOS) or Alt+F4 (for Windows). This forms a fully functional AWT application.

To convert the application to Swing, we will begin by declaring a package for the application. Although the inclusion of a package declaration is advisable when preparing to create a JAR file, it is not strictly necessary at this stage if the JAR file is not immediately required.

Next, we will convert the AWT components and containers to their corresponding Swing components by adding a "J" prefix to each. For instance, we will use JFrame, JPanel, JLabel, JTextField, and JButton instead of their AWT counterparts. However, the layout managers will remain unchanged. For example, GridLayout should not have a "J" prefix as there is no equivalent Swing-specific layout manager.

To better illustrate the difference between AWT and Swing, a comparison can be made between the two versions of the same code. When running the AWT version on a Windows machine, the buttons and other UI elements appear less visually appealing compared to their Swing counterparts. Swing offers a more refined appearance, with customizable features such as background colors that provide a more modern look and feel. While the difference in appearance is subtle on macOS, the distinction is more noticeable on Windows.

Figure 11.3 Runtime Comparison between AWT and Swing Version

To initiate the conversion of our calculator application, we begin by modifying the component and container declarations, adding the "J" prefix where appropriate, both in the declarations and within the constructor, where components and containers are instantiated. This transforms them into Swing-based components. Importantly, no changes should be made to the layout managers, as Swing does not provide its own versions.

Regarding the close button handler, there is an option to retain the existing functionality, or it may be modified to use Swing’s frame method for closing. Once the changes are saved, we can compile the code (using javac SimpleCalculator.java), and the application will now operate as a Swing-based component.

While the general appearance remains similar to the AWT version, the use of Swing provides enhanced functionality, and the UI elements—such as buttons—should now work as expected, including the "clear" and "close" buttons.

11.3Common Swing Components

11.3.1JCheckBox: RGBCheckBox.java

The JCheckBox class in Java is a part of the Swing package, which provides a way to create checkboxes in a graphical user interface. These checkboxes can be either selected or deselected by the user. Unlike radio buttons, multiple checkboxes can be selected at the same time.

In the example RGBCheckBox.java given below, we will create a simple graphical interface with three checkboxes—Red, Green, and Blue—using Swing components. We will also add a button labeled "Click Me!" for further interaction.

Code Breakdown

1.Imports: The program starts by importing java.awt.* and javax.swing.*, which provide the necessary classes for creating the GUI components and handling the layout, the java.awt package is required for the layout managers.

import java.awt.*;

import javax.swing.*;

2.Class declaration: The class RGBCheckBox is declared as a public class. Inside this class, we define private fields for the JFrame, JButton, and JCheckBox components that will make up the UI.

public class RGBCheckBox {

   private JFrame f;

   private JButton b;

   private JCheckBox red, green, blue;

3.Constructor: The constructor RGBCheckBox() initializes the JFrame and JButton objects and creates three checkboxes: red, green, and blue. These components will be part of the user interface.

public RGBCheckBox() {

   f = new JFrame("JCheckBox Example");

   b = new JButton("Click Me!");

   red = new JCheckBox(" Red ");

   green = new JCheckBox(" Green ");

   blue = new JCheckBox(" Blue ");

}

4.StartApp method: The startApp() method configures the layout of the frame, which uses a GridLayout with 4 rows and 1 column to display the checkboxes and the button vertically. The setSelected(true) method is used to pre-select the Red and Blue checkboxes.

The setLayout(new GridLayout(4, 1)) ensures that the components are arranged in four rows.

The f.add() method adds the components to the frame in the desired order.

f.setBounds(100, 100, 300, 200) specifies the position (100,100) of the top-left corner of the window and its size (300x200).

The f.setVisible(true) makes the window visible to the user.

public void startApp() {

   f.setLayout(new GridLayout(4, 1));

   red.setSelected(true);

   blue.setSelected(true);

   f.add(red);

   f.add(green);

   f.add(blue);

   f.add(b);

   f.setBounds(100, 100, 300, 200);

   f.setVisible(true);

}

5.Main method: The main method serves as the entry point for the program. It creates an instance of the RGBCheckBox class and calls the startApp() method to display the UI.

public static void main(String args[]) {

   RGBCheckBox rgb = new RGBCheckBox();

   rgb.startApp();

}

How the Code Works

When the program runs, a window appears with three checkboxes: Red, Green, and Blue. The Red and Blue checkboxes are pre-selected. Users can check or uncheck any combination of these boxes.

A button labeled "Click Me!" is also displayed, though it currently has no functionality implemented. Future extensions could involve adding event listeners to the button and checkboxes to perform actions when clicked.

Figure 11.4 RGBCheckBox Runtime

Key points

●JCheckBox is part of the Swing framework, and it inherits many methods from its superclass, allowing for extensive customization.

●The setBounds() method is used to both position and size the window, offering more control over its layout.

This simple example demonstrates how to create a basic GUI with multiple checkboxes using Swing components in Java. You can further extend this by adding event handling to make the UI interactive.

11.3.2JRadioButton: RGBRadioButton.java

In this explanation, we will break down how to create a basic Java Swing application using JRadioButton components, showing the difference between radio buttons and checkboxes.

Key Difference Between Radio Buttons and Checkboxes

●Radio buttons: Allow the user to select only one option at a time. When you select a radio button, any previously selected button in the same group is automatically deselected.

●Checkboxes (JCheckBox): Allow the user to select multiple options simultaneously. You can select or deselect multiple checkboxes independently.

Code Breakdown

1.Class and import statements: We start by importing the necessary packages:

// For GridLayout and other layout managers

import java.awt.*;

// For JFrame, JButton, JRadioButton

import javax.swing.*;

2.Creating the main class: In this case, the class is called RGBRadioButton:

public class RGBRadioButton {

   // Declare the components:

   // JFrame, JButton, and JRadioButton

   private JFrame f;

   private JButton b;

   private JRadioButton red, green, blue;

   // Constructor to initialize the components

   public RGBRadioButton() {

     f = new JFrame("RGBJRadioButton Example");

     red = new JRadioButton(" Red "); // Red

   green = new JRadioButton(" Green ");// Green

   blue = new JRadioButton(" Blue "); // Blue

   b = new JButton("Click Me!"); // Button

  }

}

3.The startApp method: This method sets up the layout and adds the components (radio buttons, buttons, etc.) to the frame:

public void startApp() {

   // Set a GridLayout with 4 rows and 1 column for

   // arranging components vertically

   f.setLayout(new GridLayout(4, 1));

   // By default, the Red radio button will

   // be selected at startup

   red.setSelected(true);

   // Add the radio buttons to the frame

   // so they appear in the UI

   f.add(red);

   f.add(green);

   f.add(blue);

   // Group the radio buttons together to ensure only

   // one can be selected at a time

   ButtonGroup colorGroup = new ButtonGroup();

   // add the red, green and blue

   // buttons to the group

   colorGroup.add(red);

   colorGroup.add(green);

   colorGroup.add(blue);

   // Add the "Click Me!" button to the frame

   f.add(b);

   // Set the size and location of the frame

   f.setBounds(200, 200, 300, 200);

   // Make the frame visible to the user

   f.setVisible(true);

}

4.Main method: This method is the entry point of the program. It creates an instance of the RGBRadioButton class and calls the startApp() method to launch the application.

public static void main(String args[]) {

   RGBRadioButton rgb = new RGBRadioButton();

   rgb.startApp(); // Start the application

}

Key Concepts

●JRadioButton: Represents a radio button in Swing. Only one button in a group of radio buttons can be selected at a time. If one is selected, the other is automatically deselected.

●ButtonGroup: Groups the radio buttons together. Without this, each radio button would function independently, meaning multiple selections could be made.

●GridLayout: This layout manager arranges components in a grid of rows and columns. In this case, we use a 4x1 grid to display three radio buttons and a button vertically.

●setSelected(true): This method pre-selects the Red radio button when the application starts.

●setBounds(): Defines the frame's position and size on the screen. In this case, the frame starts at (200, 200) with a width of 300 and a height of 200 pixels.

Grouping Radio Buttons

To make sure that only one radio button can be selected at a time, the buttons are grouped using a ButtonGroup. When the buttons are added to the group, it ensures mutual exclusivity:

ButtonGroup colorGroup = new ButtonGroup();

// add the red, green and blue buttons to the group

colorGroup.add(red);

colorGroup.add(green);

colorGroup.add(blue);

Visual Representation and Interaction

When you run the program, you'll see:

●Three radio buttons labeled Red, Green, and Blue

●A button labeled "Click Me!"

●The Red radio button is pre-selected by default

Clicking on any other radio button will automatically deselect the current selection, ensuring only one option is active at any given time.

Figure 11.5 RGBRadioButton Runtime

Exit Behavior

In Swing, even when the close button is clicked on the window, the application may not fully terminate unless a specific code is added to handle the window closure. The default behavior is that the window will hide but not exit unless specified otherwise.

11.3.3JComboBox: JComboBoxExample.java

A JComboBox in Java is a Swing component that allows users to select an item from a drop-down list. It can either be a non-editable list where users pick from predefined values or an editable one where users can also type their own input. This component combines the functionality of a button and a text field, making it a versatile input method for users.

In this example, we’ll walk through how to create a basic JComboBox, populate it with values, and implement event handling so that when a user selects an option, it updates a label to reflect the chosen value.

Components Used in the Code

●JFrame: A window or container that holds all the components of the application.

●JButton: A clickable button that triggers an event.

●JComboBox: The drop-down list that contains options for users to select from.

●JLabel: A label to display messages or results based on user actions.

●String Array: An array containing a list of colors, which will be displayed in the JComboBox.

Code Breakdown

1. Declaring the class

The class JComboBoxExample starts by declaring private variables to represent the JFrame, JButton, JComboBox, and JLabel, which will be used throughout the application.

private JFrame f;

private JButton b;

private JComboBox<String> cb;

private JLabel label;

private String colorList[];

●f represents the frame or window.

●b is the button labeled "Show".

●cb is the JComboBox containing color options.

●label will display the selected color.

●colorList[] holds the predefined color values for the JComboBox.

2. Constructor setup

The constructor initializes all the components of the GUI (Graphical User Interface). It creates the frame, button, JComboBox, and label, while also assigning positions using the setBounds() method, which defines their location and size within the frame.

public JComboBoxExample() {

   f = new JFrame("JComboBox List Example");

   label = new JLabel();

   colorList = new String[] {"Red", "Green",

            "Blue", "Yellow", "Purple"};

   cb = new JComboBox<>(colorList);

cb.setBounds(50, 100, 90, 20);

   label.setHorizontalAlignment(JLabel.CENTER);

   label.setSize(400, 100);

   b = new JButton("Show");

   b.setBounds(200, 100, 75, 20);

}

Here’s what happens:

●A new JFrame is created with the title "JComboBox List Example".

●The JLabel is aligned to the center, and its size is set.

●The JComboBox is populated with the values from the colorList array.

●The JButton labeled "Show" is created.

3. Starting the application

The startApp() method is responsible for adding the components to the frame and making the frame visible.

public void startApp() {

   f.setLayout(null);    // No layout manager is used,

                         // so positions are set manually

                         // with setBounds.

   f.add(cb);            // Add JComboBox to the frame.

   f.add(label);        // Add label to the frame.

   f.add(b);            // Add button to the frame.

   f.setSize(350, 350); // Set the size of the frame.

   f.setVisible(true);  // Make the frame visible.

}

The method also disables the default layout manager by calling f.setLayout(null), allowing manual positioning of components.

4. Event handling for the button

To make the button functional, an ActionListener is added. When the button is clicked, the selected item from the JComboBox is retrieved and displayed in the JLabel.

b.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {

   public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent ae) {

      String str = "My Color List: "

          + cb.getItemAt(cb.getSelectedIndex());

      label.setText(str); // Update the label with

             // the selected color.

   }

});

●The ActionListener listens for a button click.

●When the button is clicked, the selected value from the JComboBox is retrieved using cb.getSelectedIndex() and is set in the label.

●The label text is updated with the selected color name.

5. Main method

The main method creates an instance of the JComboBoxExample class and starts the application by calling startApp().

public static void main(String args[]) {

   JComboBoxExample jcbe = new JComboBoxExample();

   jcbe.startApp();

}

Output and Behavior

When the application is run:

●A window (JFrame) appears with a JComboBox containing the color options.

●The user can select a color from the drop-down.

●Upon clicking the "Show" button, the selected color is displayed on the label.
